posts.image_prompt: A narrow carved stone tunnel deep underground in soft volcanic rock, lit by flickering oil lamps, a huge round millstone-like stone door set into the wall, chambers branching off into darkness, cinematic
posts.caption:
🕳️ A MAN KNOCKED DOWN A WALL AND FOUND A CITY

In 1963, a resident of Derinkuyu in Cappadocia, Turkey, was renovating his home. When he broke through a basement wall, he found a hidden passage.

It led to an entire underground city.

Derinkuyu goes down roughly 280 feet and has at least 18 levels. Historians estimate it could shelter up to 20,000 people, along with stables, storage and even a church.

Huge stone doors could seal it from the inside. Dozens of ventilation shafts carried fresh air deep underground.

Its origins may reach back to around the 8th century BC, and it was expanded over the centuries, at least into the Byzantine era. People still used it as a refuge into the early 20th century.

Nobody knows exactly who dug the first tunnel.

Would you have lived underground to stay safe?
posts.image_headline: A wall hid an underground city

posts.title: The king who crashed the price of gold

scenes.image_prompt: A long royal caravan of camels and richly dressed travelers crossing golden Sahara dunes at sunrise, banners fluttering, cinematic wide shot
scenes.narration: In thirteen twenty-four, one king spent so much gold its value crashed.

posts.caption:
👑 One pilgrimage. So much gold that its price fell.

In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali passed through Cairo on his way to Mecca. The scholar al-Umari recorded that gold lost value there for years afterwards.

Was he history's richest person? Weigh in 👇

posts.image_prompt: A small square ancient steatite stamp seal carved with a bull-like animal and a few small abstract symbols above it, resting on sand at a mud-brick excavation site, warm afternoon light, macro photography
posts.caption:
🔍 A GREAT CIVILIZATION WHOSE WRITING NO ONE CAN READ

The Indus Valley Civilization built planned cities in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. Its writing flourished around 2600–1900 BC.

Archaeologists have found thousands of short inscriptions, mostly on small stone stamp seals, from dozens of sites.

The problem? They are tiny. The average inscription is only about five signs long, and none found so far is longer than about 26.

There are roughly 400 different signs, and there's no agreement on what language they record. No bilingual inscription — like Egypt's Rosetta Stone — has ever been found to help.

Do you think the Indus script will ever be deciphered?

posts.title: The shipwreck that started a race for longitude
posts.hook_text: ON THIS DAY: A FLEET HIT ROCKS

scenes.image_prompt: Wooden warships of 1707 smashing onto jagged black rocks in a stormy night sea, lantern lights, crashing white surf
scenes.narration: On this night in 1707, a whole British fleet hit the rocks.

scenes.image_prompt: A fleet of 18th-century warships under full sail in fog, sailing toward a dim rocky coastline, grey dusk
scenes.narration: Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell was bringing his warships home to England. In the dark, they reached the Isles of Scilly.
scenes.label: SCILLY

scenes.image_prompt: Navigators in tricorn hats bent over a sea chart with dividers by lamplight, worried faces
scenes.narration: The navigators believed they were clear of land. They were wrong about where they were.

scenes.image_prompt: A massive warship splitting on a reef, masts falling, tiny lifeboat in towering waves
scenes.narration: Four ships were lost. More than thirteen hundred men died, including the admiral himself.

scenes.image_prompt: An 18th-century Parliament chamber with men in powdered wigs debating, a scroll reading a reward notice
scenes.narration: The disaster became famous. In 1714, Parliament offered up to twenty thousand pounds to anyone who could find a ship's longitude at sea.

scenes.image_prompt: A beautifully crafted brass and wood marine clock with intricate gears on a velvet table, soft workshop light
scenes.narration: A clockmaker named John Harrison spent decades building sea clocks to solve it.
scenes.label: JOHN HARRISON

scenes.image_prompt: Old nautical charts with faded coastlines spread on a table, a brass compass and candle on top
scenes.narration: The twist? Historians now doubt longitude alone was to blame. Poor charts, currents and bad compasses may have mattered just as much.

scenes.image_prompt: Calm sea at dawn over the jagged Western Rocks of Scilly, gulls, no ships
scenes.narration: Human error or impossible conditions? Tell us. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🌊 ON THIS DAY in 1707, a British fleet sailed straight onto the rocks of the Isles of Scilly.

Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell's navigators thought they were safely clear of land. Four ships were lost and well over a thousand men died, the admiral among them.

The disaster helped push Parliament to pass the Longitude Act of 1714, offering up to £20,000 for a reliable way to find longitude at sea — the challenge clockmaker John Harrison spent his life on.

But historians now argue over the cause: longitude, bad charts, currents or compasses. Which do you think sank the fleet? 👇
